title: Star Schema: Joins and Query Speed
description: An analytics team needs fast, simple queries across a sales dataset. They can choose between a star schema and a fully normalised relational schema. Which statement best explains why a star schema is preferred for analytical queries?
options: A star schema denormalises dimension data into flat tables, reducing the number of joins needed and speeding up analytical queries
A star schema stores data in a single giant table with no joins at all, making reads as fast as possible
A star schema enforces strict third normal form across all tables, which improves query optimiser performance
A star schema is preferred because it compresses data more aggressively than a normalised schema
explanation: A star schema places a central fact table surrounded by denormalised dimension tables. Because each dimension is already flat (not further broken into sub-tables), most queries require only a single join between the fact table and one or more dimensions — far fewer joins than a fully normalised schema. Option B is wrong: a star schema still uses joins; it is not a single flat table. Option C is wrong: star schemas typically violate 3NF intentionally by denormalising. Option D is wrong: compression is a storage-layer concern unrelated to schema shape.
hints: Think about how many tables a typical analytical query must touch in each schema design.
Star schemas intentionally flatten dimension data to trade storage for fewer joins.

title: Snowflake Schema: Dimension Normalisation
description: A data warehouse team notices their product dimension contains repetitive category and subcategory text repeated across thousands of rows. They split category into its own table linked back to the product table. What schema pattern have they moved toward?
options: A snowflake schema, where dimension tables are normalised into additional sub-dimension tables
A star schema, where each dimension is stored as a single denormalised flat table
A data vault, where hubs track business keys and satellites hold descriptive attributes
A wide-table design, where all attributes are collapsed into a single row per entity
explanation: Normalising a dimension by breaking a repeated attribute (category) into its own table is the defining characteristic of a snowflake schema — dimension tables have child tables, forming a snowflake-like branching structure. Option B describes a star schema, which keeps dimensions flat and denormalised. Option C describes data vault, a completely different methodology. Option D describes a wide-table (one-big-table) approach, which is the opposite of normalisation.
hints: Consider what happens to the shape of the schema when you split a dimension table into two linked tables.
The snowflake schema is named for the branching, multi-level dimension structure that results from normalising dimensions.

title: Star vs Snowflake: Storage and Joins
description: A team debates whether to use a star schema or a snowflake schema for a new data mart. Which trade-off correctly describes the difference between the two?
options: Star schemas use more storage due to repeated dimension data but require fewer joins; snowflake schemas save storage by normalising dimensions but require more joins
Star schemas require more joins than snowflake schemas because their fact tables are larger
Snowflake schemas always outperform star schemas for analytical queries because normalised data is smaller
Star schemas and snowflake schemas are functionally identical; the difference is only cosmetic naming
explanation: The classic star vs snowflake trade-off is storage efficiency versus query simplicity. Star schemas repeat dimension attributes (e.g., country name) across many rows, wasting space, but queries hit fewer tables. Snowflake schemas normalise those repeated values into sub-tables, saving storage, but queries need additional joins. Option B is backwards — star schemas have fewer joins, not more. Option C is wrong: fewer joins often means faster analytical queries even if individual tables are smaller. Option D is wrong: the structural difference has real performance implications.
hints: Think about what happens to duplicated text values in a dimension when you normalise versus when you flatten.
Fewer joins typically mean simpler and faster analytical queries for end users.

title: First Normal Form: Repeating Groups
description: A database table has an `order_items` column that stores a comma-separated list of product IDs (e.g., '101,205,309') within a single cell. Which normalisation problem does this violate, and what is the fix?
options: It violates First Normal Form by storing multiple values in one cell; the fix is to give each product ID its own row
It violates Second Normal Form because the product IDs are partially dependent on a composite key
It violates Third Normal Form because the product IDs create a transitive dependency on the order total
It violates Boyce-Codd Normal Form because the product IDs determine the primary key
explanation: First Normal Form (1NF) requires that every column contains atomic (indivisible) values — no repeating groups or multi-value cells. Storing a comma-separated list in a single cell is a classic 1NF violation. The fix is to move each product ID to its own row (or a separate junction table). Options B and C are wrong: 2NF and 3NF deal with functional dependencies between columns, which is not the issue here. Option D is wrong: BCNF concerns candidate key determinants, not multi-value columns.
hints: Ask yourself: can you sort or filter on a single product ID in this column without parsing the string first?
First Normal Form requires each cell to hold exactly one value — atomic and indivisible.

title: Second Normal Form: Partial Dependencies
description: An `order_items` table has a composite primary key of (`order_id`, `product_id`). The table also includes a `product_name` column. The product name depends only on `product_id`, not on the full composite key. Which normal form is violated?
options: Second Normal Form, because product_name depends on only part of the composite primary key
First Normal Form, because product_name contains text values rather than numeric identifiers
Third Normal Form, because product_name transitively depends on order_id through product_id
No normal form is violated; this is a standard and acceptable table design
explanation: Second Normal Form (2NF) requires that every non-key column is fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key. Here the primary key is (`order_id`, `product_id`), but `product_name` depends only on `product_id` — a partial dependency. The fix is to move `product_name` to a separate Products table keyed by `product_id`. Option B is wrong: 1NF is about atomic values, not data types. Option C is wrong: a transitive dependency would involve a non-key column depending on another non-key column. Option D is wrong: this is a genuine 2NF violation.
hints: Check whether every non-key column needs both parts of the composite key to be uniquely identified.

Ask: could you look up `product_name` knowing only `product_id`, without needing `order_id` at all? If yes, the column does not depend on the whole composite key — think about which normal form governs that requirement.

title: Third Normal Form: Transitive Dependencies
description: An `employees` table has columns: `employee_id` (PK), `department_id`, and `department_name`. `department_name` is determined by `department_id`, not directly by `employee_id`. Which normal form is violated, and what is the recommended fix?
options: Third Normal Form is violated; move department_name to a separate Departments table keyed by department_id
Second Normal Form is violated; remove department_id and keep only department_name in the employees table
First Normal Form is violated; department_name contains a multi-word string which is not atomic
No normal form is violated; storing department_name alongside department_id is a useful denormalisation
explanation: Third Normal Form (3NF) requires that every non-key column depends directly on the primary key, not on another non-key column. Here `department_name` depends on `department_id` (a non-key column), creating a transitive dependency: `employee_id` → `department_id` → `department_name`. The fix is a separate Departments table. Option B is wrong: removing `department_id` would lose the relationship entirely. Option C is wrong: 1NF is about multi-value cells, not string length. Option D is wrong: while denormalisation is sometimes intentional, it does violate 3NF.
hints: Trace the dependency chain: does department_name depend on the primary key directly, or through another column?
A transitive dependency exists when a non-key column determines another non-key column.

title: Transaction Fact Table: One Row Per Event
description: A retail company wants to record every individual purchase event — capturing which customer bought which product, at what price, and at what time. Which type of fact table is most appropriate?
options: A transaction fact table, which stores one row per discrete business event (each purchase)
A periodic snapshot fact table, which records the state of metrics at regular time intervals
An accumulating snapshot fact table, which tracks a business process across multiple milestones
A dimension table, which stores descriptive attributes about products and customers
explanation: A transaction fact table is purpose-built for recording individual business events at the moment they occur — exactly one row per event. Retail purchases are a textbook use case. Option B describes a periodic snapshot (e.g., daily inventory balance), which aggregates over a period, not per event. Option C describes an accumulating snapshot used for multi-stage processes like order fulfilment pipelines. Option D is wrong: a dimension table stores descriptive attributes, not transactional measurements.
hints: Consider whether you need to capture each event individually or summarise over a period of time.
Transaction fact tables are the most granular type — one row per discrete event as it happens.

title: Periodic Snapshot Fact Table
description: A finance team needs a table that captures the total account balance for every bank account at the end of each business day, regardless of whether any transactions occurred that day. Which fact table type fits this requirement?
options: A periodic snapshot fact table, which records the state of a measure at regular, predefined time intervals
A transaction fact table, which inserts a new row for every individual debit or credit event
An accumulating snapshot fact table, which tracks multi-stage milestones for each account
A dimension table with a date attribute capturing balance history
explanation: A periodic snapshot fact table records the state of one or more measures at fixed time intervals (daily, weekly, monthly). Daily account balances are a classic use case: a row exists for every account for every day, even if no transactions occurred. Option B (transaction fact) only records events; if no transaction happened, nothing is stored, leaving gaps. Option C (accumulating snapshot) tracks process milestones like loan approval stages, not time-periodic balances. Option D is wrong: balance history over time is a fact, not a dimension attribute.
hints: Think about whether you need to capture a point-in-time measurement on a schedule, or only when something changes.
Periodic snapshots ensure a row exists for every period — even quiet days with no activity.

title: Accumulating Snapshot Fact Table
description: An e-commerce company tracks orders through five stages: placed, payment confirmed, warehoused, shipped, and delivered. Each order has a single row that gets updated as it moves through each stage, recording the date each milestone is reached. Which fact table type is this?
options: An accumulating snapshot fact table, which tracks the progress of a business process through defined milestones
A transaction fact table, which records a new row at each individual stage transition
A periodic snapshot fact table, which records order state at the end of each business day
A slowly changing dimension, which records historical changes to order attributes over time
explanation: An accumulating snapshot fact table is designed for business processes that have a well-defined lifecycle with multiple milestone dates. Each entity (here, each order) gets one row, and that row is updated as milestones are reached — date columns are filled in as stages complete. Option B describes a transaction fact table, which would create a new row per stage transition. Option C describes a periodic snapshot, which records fixed-interval snapshots independent of process stages. Option D is wrong: slowly changing dimensions track attribute history for dimension records, not process milestones.
hints: Consider whether each entity gets one row that is updated, or whether every event creates a new row.
Accumulating snapshots are ideal when a process has a fixed number of known stages and you want to track how long each stage takes.

title: Surrogate Key vs Natural Key: Identity Source
description: A customer dimension table uses the customer's email address as its primary key. A colleague suggests replacing it with a system-generated integer key. What is the primary benefit of the system-generated integer key?
options: It remains stable even if the customer's email address changes, preventing broken references in fact tables
It is more human-readable, making it easier for analysts to look up individual customers
It guarantees uniqueness across the source system, because email addresses can collide
It improves data security by making it impossible to identify customers from the key alone
explanation: A system-generated (surrogate) key is a stable, internally assigned identifier that does not change when business attributes change. If a customer changes their email, a surrogate key keeps all fact table references intact. Option B is wrong: integer keys are less readable than email addresses — readability is an argument for natural keys. Option C is wrong: surrogate keys do not improve source-system uniqueness guarantees; that is an application-level concern. Option D is wrong: while surrogate keys do obscure identity, security is a side benefit, not the primary purpose.
hints: Ask what happens to the fact table rows if a customer updates their email and the email is the primary key.
Surrogate keys are generated by the warehouse, so they stay constant regardless of changes to source system data.

title: Natural Key: When Source IDs Are Reliable
description: A team is building a product dimension. Products are identified by a UPC barcode that is globally unique, never reused, and does not change once assigned. The team debates using the UPC as the primary key versus generating a surrogate integer. Which argument favours using the UPC as the natural key?
options: The UPC is already stable and globally unique, so a surrogate key adds complexity with no meaningful benefit
The UPC should never be used as a key because natural keys always change over time
A surrogate key is always required in a dimensional model regardless of the properties of the natural key
The UPC cannot serve as a primary key because it is a string, and primary keys must be integers
explanation: Surrogate keys exist primarily to handle instability and non-uniqueness in natural keys. When a natural key is already guaranteed to be stable, globally unique, and never reused (like a UPC barcode), the surrogate key provides little additional value and adds join complexity. Option B is wrong: it falsely asserts that natural keys always change — many do not. Option C is wrong: surrogate keys are a best practice in dimensional modeling but are not an absolute requirement when the natural key is reliable. Option D is wrong: string columns are perfectly valid primary keys.
hints: Consider the two situations where a system-generated key adds real value over a business identifier — does either situation apply to a UPC barcode?
If a natural key is already stable and unique, adding a system-generated key creates overhead without solving a real problem.

title: Surrogate Key: Integrating Multiple Source Systems
description: A company merges with a competitor. Both companies had their own CRM systems, each numbering customers starting from 1. The data warehouse must integrate both customer datasets. Why is a surrogate key essential in this situation?
options: Customer IDs from both systems collide (both start at 1), so a warehouse-generated surrogate key provides a unique identifier across all sources
Surrogate keys allow the warehouse to delete duplicate customers automatically on load
Natural keys from source systems are never allowed in a data warehouse, making surrogate keys mandatory
A surrogate key allows analysts to trace a customer record back to its original source system
explanation: When two source systems use overlapping ID sequences (both starting at customer_id = 1), the same natural key value refers to different customers. A warehouse-generated surrogate key — unique within the warehouse — resolves the collision and allows both datasets to coexist without ambiguity. Option B is wrong: surrogate keys do not deduplicate records; that requires explicit matching logic. Option C is wrong: natural keys can and often do appear in warehouses as attributes alongside a surrogate key. Option D is a real capability of the source system code (often stored alongside the surrogate), but it is not why surrogate keys are essential here.
hints: Consider what happens when two source systems produce the same ID number for completely different customers.
Surrogate keys are assigned by the warehouse, so they are always unique within the warehouse regardless of source system values.

title: SCD Type 1: Overwrite With No History
description: A customer moves to a new city. The data warehouse team updates the `city` column in the customer dimension to the new city name, overwriting the old value. No record of the previous city is kept. Which slowly changing dimension strategy is being used?
options: Type 1 — overwrite the old value; historical values are lost
Type 2 — add a new row for the new city; the old row is expired with an end date
Type 3 — add a new column (previous_city) to store the old value alongside the current value
Type 0 — the value is fixed at load and never updated regardless of changes in the source
explanation: SCD Type 1 simply overwrites the attribute with the new value. No history is preserved — the old city is gone. This is appropriate when historical accuracy of the attribute is not needed (e.g., correcting a data entry error). Option B describes Type 2, which preserves history by versioning rows. Option C describes Type 3, which adds a column for the most recent previous value. Option D describes Type 0 (or 'fixed'), where the attribute never changes once loaded.
hints: Think about whether any historical record of the old city would remain after the update.
The simplest strategy overwrites the existing value directly — no new rows, no extra columns.

title: SCD Type 2: Preserving History With New Rows
description: A sales analyst needs to report revenue by the sales region a customer belonged to at the time of each purchase — not their current region. The customer may have moved between regions over time. Which dimension handling strategy supports this requirement?
options: Add a new dimension row each time the region changes, with effective start and end dates, and link fact rows to the row that was current at purchase time
Overwrite the region column each time it changes and recalculate all historical reports using the current region
Add a previous_region column to the customer dimension to track the single most recent change
Store region in the fact table instead of the dimension so it is captured at the time of purchase
explanation: When you need to report historical facts against the dimension value that was accurate at the time of the transaction, you need row versioning — the defining feature of SCD Type 2. Each version gets a surrogate key and effective date range; fact rows reference the surrogate key of the current version at the time of the event. Option B (Type 1) destroys the historical region, making accurate historical reporting impossible. Option C (Type 3) only remembers one previous value and cannot handle multiple changes. Option D places the attribute in the fact table, which works for a single attribute but is not a scalable or standard dimensional modeling approach.
hints: Consider which approach lets you look at a fact row and determine exactly which region was active when that sale occurred.
Row versioning with effective dates means every historical state of the dimension is preserved as a separate record.

title: SCD Type 1 vs Type 2: Choosing the Right Strategy
description: A data team is updating the customer dimension. For `email_address`, history is irrelevant — the team only needs the current contact information. For `customer_segment` (e.g., Gold, Silver), historical accuracy matters for revenue attribution. Which combination is correct?
options: Type 1 for email_address (overwrite); Type 2 for customer_segment (add versioned rows)
Type 2 for email_address (add versioned rows); Type 1 for customer_segment (overwrite)
Type 1 for both columns, since overwriting is simpler and analytics rarely require history
Type 2 for both columns, since preserving all history is always safer and more flexible
explanation: Different attributes in the same dimension can — and should — use different SCD strategies based on business need. Email address is a contact detail where only the current value matters (Type 1). Customer segment directly affects revenue attribution and reporting accuracy, so historical versions must be preserved (Type 2). Option B reverses the logic. Option C sacrifices the analytics accuracy that segment history provides. Option D applies Type 2 to everything including email, which inflates row counts unnecessarily for attributes where history has no analytical value.
hints: Ask for each attribute: does a historical report ever need to know what this value was in the past?
Mixing Type 1 and Type 2 within the same dimension is a common and valid pattern in practice.

title: Grain Definition: What One Row Represents
description: A fact table is being designed for retail sales. A team member says: 'The grain is one row per order.' Another says: 'The grain is one row per line item within an order.' Why does this distinction matter?
options: The grain determines what facts and dimensions can be associated with each row — a finer grain (line item) allows tracking individual products but creates more rows than an order-level grain
The grain is just a documentation convention; it has no impact on the physical structure or query results
A coarser grain (order-level) always produces more accurate analytics than a finer grain (line item)
The grain must match the granularity of the source system exactly and cannot be changed during modelling
explanation: Grain defines the level of detail represented by a single row in a fact table. Choosing order-level grain means one row per order: you can store order-level facts (total amount, discount) but cannot track which specific products were purchased. Line-item grain allows product-level facts (quantity, unit price per product) but results in many more rows. The grain decision drives which dimensions and measures are meaningful. Option B is wrong: grain is a structural decision with real consequences. Option C is wrong: finer grain is often more flexible and accurate, not less. Option D is wrong: the modeller chooses grain based on analytical needs, not source system structure.
hints: Ask what a single row in the fact table represents — can an order-level row tell you how many units of a specific product were sold?
The level of detail in a fact table — what one row represents — is the single most important design decision and must be declared explicitly before adding columns.

title: Grain Consistency: Mixing Granularities
description: A fact table is defined at the grain of one row per sales order line item. A new requirement asks to add a `monthly_sales_target` column that is set once per salesperson per month. What problem does adding this column directly to the line-item fact table cause?
options: The monthly target value would be repeated on every line item for that salesperson that month, making aggregation produce inflated totals
The monthly target cannot be stored numerically in a line-item fact table and must be a text field
Adding any column to an existing fact table is not allowed; a new table must always be created
The monthly target would cause the grain to become ambiguous only if it is NULL for some rows
explanation: Adding a coarser-grained measure (monthly target, set once per month per salesperson) to a finer-grained fact table (per line item) causes fan-out inflation: if a salesperson has 50 line items in a month, the monthly target appears on all 50 rows. SUM(monthly_sales_target) would return 50x the actual target. The correct approach is to store the target in a separate fact table at the correct grain (month/salesperson) and join when needed. Option B is wrong: data type is unrelated to this issue. Option C is wrong: adding columns is allowed but must preserve grain integrity. Option D is wrong: the problem exists even without NULLs.
hints: Consider what SUM(monthly_sales_target) would return if the target value appears on every line item for the month.
Each measure in a fact table should be naturally defined at the declared grain — not at a coarser or finer level.

title: Denormalisation: Read Performance in OLAP
description: An analytics team frequently runs reports that join a sales fact table to a customer dimension and then to a region table linked from customer. Response times are slow. A colleague suggests merging the region table into the customer dimension. What is the primary benefit of this denormalisation?
options: Queries need one fewer join, reducing query complexity and improving read performance
Denormalising the region into the customer table enforces that each customer can belong to only one region
Merging the tables reduces storage cost by eliminating duplicate region rows
Denormalisation improves write performance by reducing the number of tables that must be updated on insert
explanation: The primary driver for denormalisation in an analytical (OLAP) context is read performance: fewer joins means simpler query plans and faster execution, especially at scale. Merging region into the customer dimension eliminates one join from every query that uses region. Option B is wrong: the cardinality constraint (one region per customer) is a business rule, not a result of denormalisation. Option C is wrong: merging actually duplicates region text across many customer rows, increasing storage. Option D is wrong: denormalisation typically harms write performance because updates to the redundant data must touch more rows.
hints: Count how many tables a typical region-level sales report must join before and after the merge.
In analytical workloads, reads vastly outnumber writes, so optimising for read speed is usually worth the storage trade-off.

title: Denormalisation Cost: Update Anomalies
description: A team denormalises the `region_name` into the customer dimension, so every customer row directly contains their region's display name. The company later renames a region from 'North-East' to 'Northeast'. What risk does this denormalisation create?
options: Every customer row in that region must be updated individually; if any row is missed, the dimension contains inconsistent region names
Renaming a region is impossible once data has been denormalised into the dimension table
The surrogate key for the region must be regenerated, breaking all fact table references
Denormalised tables use immutable storage, so the region name column is read-only after the first load
explanation: When a value is denormalised into many rows, any change to that value must be applied to every row that holds it. If any row is missed — due to a partial update, race condition, or ETL error — the dimension contains inconsistent data. This is an update anomaly, one of the classic downsides of denormalisation. Option B is wrong: renaming is possible, just risky and expensive. Option C is wrong: the region_name is stored as an attribute, not a key; surrogates are unaffected. Option D is wrong: there is no immutability constraint on denormalised tables.
hints: Think about how many rows would need to change if a region name is updated, versus how many rows would change in a fully normalised design.
Update anomalies are the main data quality risk introduced by denormalisation.

title: OLTP vs OLAP: Optimisation Goals
description: A company runs two database systems: one that processes thousands of short customer transactions per second (order placements, inventory updates), and one used exclusively by analysts to run long-running aggregation queries across years of historical data. Which statement correctly matches each system to its optimisation goal?
options: The transaction system is OLTP, optimised for fast, concurrent writes; the analytics system is OLAP, optimised for fast reads over large datasets
The transaction system is OLAP, because it handles many operations; the analytics system is OLTP, because queries are longer
Both systems are OLTP; the analytics system simply uses slower hardware
OLAP systems are used for both workloads; the distinction is only in the query language used
explanation: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) systems are designed for high-throughput, low-latency individual writes (inserts, updates, deletes) with strong consistency. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) systems are designed for complex, aggregated reads over large historical datasets. They typically use columnar storage, relaxed normalisation, and partitioning to speed up analytical queries. Option B swaps the definitions. Option C is wrong: analytical systems are architecturally distinct from OLTP, not just slower hardware. Option D is wrong: OLAP and OLTP are distinct architectural patterns, not just different query languages.
hints: Consider which system needs to handle many small writes per second vs. few but very wide analytical reads.
The 'O' in both stands for Online, but the 'T' (Transactional) vs 'A' (Analytical) captures the fundamental difference in workload.

title: OLAP Schema Choice: Why Not Normalise Fully?
description: A backend engineer proposes running all business analytics directly on the fully normalised OLTP database to avoid maintaining a separate data warehouse. A data engineer objects. What is the strongest argument against using the OLTP schema for analytics?
options: Analytical queries on a normalised OLTP schema require many joins and scan large volumes of rows, degrading performance and competing with live transaction writes
Normalised OLTP databases do not support SQL, so analytical queries cannot be run on them
OLTP databases automatically delete historical records to save space, making trend analysis impossible
Fully normalised schemas cannot store numeric measures, so aggregations like SUM and AVG are unavailable
explanation: OLTP schemas are normalised for write efficiency — data is split across many tables to minimise redundancy. Analytical queries need to rejoin those tables repeatedly and scan large row volumes, which is slow and locks rows needed by live transactions. A separate OLAP system (with denormalised schemas, columnar storage, and no write contention) is optimised for this workload. Option B is wrong: normalised databases absolutely support SQL and aggregation queries. Option C is wrong: OLTP systems retain historical records unless explicitly purged. Option D is wrong: numeric measures can be stored in any relational schema.
hints: Think about what happens to live order processing when a long-running analytical query scans the same tables.
The more joins a query needs, the more expensive it becomes — and normalised schemas maximise the number of joins.

title: DBT: Staging Layer Purpose
description: A dbt project has a `models/staging/` folder containing models that select from raw source tables and apply column renaming, basic type casting, and deduplication — but no business logic. What is the purpose of this staging layer?
options: To create a clean, standardised intermediate layer that decouples raw source data from business-logic models downstream
To serve as the final analytics-ready tables that BI tools query directly for dashboards
To store raw source data exactly as it arrives, with no transformations applied
To define the physical partitioning and clustering strategy for the production warehouse
explanation: The staging layer in dbt is a thin cleaning layer: it standardises column names, casts data types, and removes obvious duplicates, but applies no business logic. Its purpose is to create a stable, consistent interface between the raw source tables (which may change schema) and the downstream mart models (which encode business rules). This decoupling means that if the source schema changes, only the staging model needs to be updated. Option B describes the mart layer, which is the analytics-ready output. Option C describes the raw/source layer, which staging is meant to clean. Option D is wrong: partitioning and clustering are infrastructure concerns, not staging model responsibilities.
hints: Think about staging as a translation layer — converting source system conventions into your warehouse's conventions before any business logic is applied.
dbt projects typically follow a layered pattern: sources → staging → intermediate → mart.

title: Dimension Table: Descriptive Attributes
description: In a dimensional model for an airline, which of the following is most appropriate to store as a dimension table rather than as a column in the fact table?
options: Aircraft details — model, manufacturer, seat capacity, and cabin class configuration
Number of passengers on a flight
Revenue collected for a flight
Duration of the flight in minutes
explanation: Dimension tables store descriptive, often textual attributes used to filter, group, and label facts. Aircraft model, manufacturer, seat capacity, and cabin configuration are all stable descriptive properties of an aircraft — exactly what a dimension is for. Options B, C, and D are numeric measures that change per flight event: passenger count, revenue, and duration are facts to be stored in the fact table alongside the foreign key to the aircraft dimension. A simple rule: if it answers 'how many / how much', it is likely a fact; if it answers 'what kind / which one', it is likely a dimension attribute.
hints: Ask whether the value is something you measure about an event, or something you use to describe and categorise the entity involved.
Dimensions answer 'who, what, where, when, why' — facts answer 'how many, how much, how long'.

title: Referential Integrity: Orphaned Fact Rows
description: A fact table references a customer dimension via `customer_key`. A batch process deletes several inactive customer rows from the dimension table. What problem does this create for the fact table?
options: Fact rows that referenced the deleted customers become orphaned — they have a customer_key with no matching dimension row, breaking lookups and joins
The fact table is automatically updated to set customer_key to NULL for affected rows
The deleted dimension rows are moved to an archive table and all fact joins continue to work transparently
Deleting dimension rows has no effect on the fact table since dimension keys are denormalised into the fact
explanation: Referential integrity means every foreign key in the fact table must have a corresponding row in the referenced dimension table. Deleting dimension rows without first handling the dependent fact rows creates orphaned fact rows — joins to the customer dimension will return no results for those customers, silently dropping data from reports. Option B is wrong: most data warehouses do not automatically NULL out foreign keys on dimension deletes. Option C is wrong: there is no automatic transparent archive-and-redirect mechanism. Option D is wrong: the fact table stores the key reference, not the full denormalised attributes — the join is still required.
hints: Think about what a JOIN between the fact table and the dimension table would return for a customer_key that no longer exists in the dimension.
Before deleting dimension rows, check whether any fact rows still reference them.

title: Star Schema Design: Identifying Facts vs Dimensions
scenario_context: A streaming music company wants to build a data warehouse to analyse listening behaviour. Their source system records: song_id, song_title, artist_name, genre, user_id, user_country, subscription_tier, play_timestamp, play_duration_seconds, and was_skipped (boolean). The analytics team needs to answer questions like: how many minutes were streamed per genre per month, and which subscription tier has the highest skip rate?
description: Given the streaming company's analytics requirements, which design correctly separates facts from dimensions in a star schema?
options: Facts: play_duration_seconds, was_skipped (per play event); Dimensions: Song (song_id, title, artist, genre), User (user_id, country, subscription_tier), Date (from play_timestamp)
Facts: song_title, artist_name, genre, user_country, subscription_tier; Dimensions: play_duration_seconds, was_skipped
Facts: play_duration_seconds, was_skipped, genre, subscription_tier; Dimensions: song_id, user_id, play_timestamp
Facts: all columns in a single wide fact table with no separate dimension tables
explanation: In a star schema, facts are numeric measures of a business event (duration streamed, skip flag), and dimensions are descriptive attributes used to filter and group those measures (song metadata, user profile, date). Option A correctly identifies play_duration_seconds and was_skipped as event-level measures, and groups descriptive attributes into Song, User, and Date dimensions — enabling queries like 'minutes per genre per month' by joining fact to Date and Song dimensions. Option B inverts the design: text attributes like song_title and genre are dimensions, not facts. Option C mixes descriptive attributes (genre, subscription_tier) into the fact table, which creates the grain-mixing problem. Option D (a single wide table) works at small scale but abandons the dimensional model entirely, making it hard to add new dimensions or reuse dimension tables.
hints: Separate the event's measurements (what was counted or measured) from the entities that describe who, what, and when the event involved.
Dimensions are reusable across multiple fact tables; facts change with every event.
